title: Exploring Societal Biases in Generative AI using Social Science Constructs and Theories.
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) often reproduces and amplifies societal stereotypes, such as portraying software engineers predominantly as young, white males. Such outputs reflect biases embedded in the training data and are rooted in historical discrimination and systemic inequalities. Addressing these biases requires more than technical fixes; it demands a socio-technical perspective that combines algorithmic approaches with a critical understanding of the social contexts and ideologies in which these technologies operate. We argue that software engineering (SE) researchers and practitioners should engage with constructs and theories from the social sciences to study, explain the persistence, and support the mitigation of bias in GenAI. We collate and discuss social theories relevant to SE research and practice, highlight risks associated with blind theory transfer, and call for more systematic interdisciplinary collaboration between SE and the social sciences. By carefully grounding GenAI research into relevant social perspectives that fit the SE context in the age of AI, the SE community will be better equipped to design inclusive tools, develop equitable solutions, and articulate their societal impacts.

title: How Fair is Software Fairness Testing?
abstract: Software fairness testing is a central method for evaluating AI systems, yet the meaning of fairness is often treated as fixed and universally applicable. This vision paper positions fairness testing as culturally situated and examines the problem across three dimensions. First, fairness metrics encode particular cultural values while marginalizing others. Second, test datasets are predominantly designed from Western contexts, excluding knowledge systems grounded in oral traditions, Indigenous languages, and non-digital communities. Third, fairness testing raises ethical concerns, including the reliance on low-paid data labeling in the Global South, and associated with this, the environmental costs of training and deploying large-scale models, which disproportionately affect climate-vulnerable populations. Addressing these issues requires rethinking fairness testing beyond universal metrics and moving toward evaluation frameworks that respect cultural plurality and acknowledge the right to refuse algorithmic mediation.
